abstract: Conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) and value-at-risk (VaR) are popular tail-risk measures in finance and insurance industries as well as in highly reliable, safety-critical uncertain environments where often the underlying probability distributions are heavy-tailed. We use the multi-armed bandit best-arm identification framework and consider the problem of identifying the arm from amongst finitely many that has the smallest CVaR, VaR, or weighted sum of CVaR and mean. The latter captures the risk-return trade-off common in finance. Our main contribution is an optimal $\delta$-correct algorithm that acts on general arms, including heavy-tailed distributions, and matches the lower bound on the expected number of samples needed, asymptotically (as $ \delta$ approaches $0$). The algorithm requires solving a non-convex optimization problem in the space of probability measures, that requires delicate analysis. En-route, we develop new non-asymptotic, anytime-valid, empirical-likelihood-based concentration inequalities for tail-risk measures.
title: Optimal Best-Arm Identification Methods for Tail-Risk Measures

abstract: As future superhuman models become increasingly complex, accurately supervising their behavior may exceed human capabilities. Recent works have demonstrated that in such scenarios, weak models can effectively supervise strong models, a phenomenon known as weak-to-strong generalization. However, we find that naive weak-to-strong generalization fails under distribution shifts, often leading to worse performance of the strong model than its weak supervisors. To address this, we propose RAVEN, a robust weak-to-strong generalization framework that dynamically learns the optimal combinations of weak models in addition to parameters of the strong model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RAVEN on image classification, text classification, and preference alignment tasks. RAVEN outperforms alternative baselines by over 30% on out-of-distribution tasks while matching or surpassing existing methods on in-distribution tasks. Moreover, our results show that RAVEN assigns higher weights to more accurate weak models, demonstrating its ability to automatically identify trustworthy supervision.

summary.idea: RAVEN jointly trains the stronger model and learns how to weight multiple weak supervisors. The weighting adapts so more reliable supervision can contribute more strongly.
summary.limitations: The abstract does not specify the metric or denominator behind that percentage. Its experiments demonstrate selected distribution shifts, not guaranteed supervision of future superhuman models in every setting.
summary.problem: A stronger model trained using weaker supervisors can inherit their mistakes, especially when the test distribution changes. In the reported setting, naive supervision can make the stronger model perform worse than its teachers.
summary.results: Across image classification, text classification, and preference alignment, the method improves on compared out-of-distribution baselines by over 30% while matching or exceeding in-distribution alternatives.
summary.tldr: Learn which weak supervisors to trust while training a stronger model for changing data distributions.

title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization under Distribution Shifts
